title: Delayed and conquered: Phaseout and renaissance of the Swedish nuclear power regime
text: Delayed and conquered: Phaseout and renaissance of the Swedish nuclear power regime. Sweden represents the first national attempt to phase out nuclear power. Following a 1980 referendum, the policy was partially implemented but never completed. Today, nuclear power has re-emerged as a cornerstone of plans for large-scale electricity system expansion. This paper examines the volatile dynamics of phaseouts by tracing the emergence, weakening and reversal of the Swedish nuclear phaseout. It argues that delay provides a productive lens for understanding how adopted phaseout mandates can lose force over time. The analysis centers on three clusters of delay mechanisms. First, the Swedish phaseout strategy institutionalized incrementalism, avoiding far-reaching commitments in favor of small, stepwise decisions guided by the best available knowledge. This made knowledge production central to implementation, but also turned epistemic uncertainties, tradeoffs and policy decision thresholds into mechanisms of delay. Second, market deregulation shifted the institutional foundation of the phaseout by embedding implementation more firmly in market coordination, thereby delaying deliberate decommissioning. Third, implementation delays, implementation deficits and procedural delays associated with public inquiries further weakened the phaseout trajectory. Over time, these delays accumulated: nuclear power remained central to the electricity system, while the space for alternative sociotechnical configurations remained constrained. As external conditions shifted and the electricity system experienced a shock, nuclear power was first maintained and later repositioned for expansion. These findings suggest that phaseouts, especially when organized around incremental decision-making, are structurally vulnerable to delay, with implications for ongoing technology phaseouts elsewhere.

title: Nuclear Power: A Hedge against Uncertain Gas and Carbon Prices?
text: Nuclear Power: A Hedge against Uncertain Gas and Carbon Prices?. High fossil fuel prices have rekindled interest in nuclear power. This paper identifies specific characteristics making nuclear power unattractive to merchant generators in liberalized electricity markets, and argues that non-fossil fuel technologies have an overlooked ‘option value’ given fuel and carbon price uncertainty. Stochastic optimization estimates the company option value of keeping open the choice between nuclear and gas technologies. The merchant option value decreases sharply as the correlation between electricity, gas, and carbon prices rises, casting doubt on whether merchant investors have adequate incentives to choose socially efficient diversification in liberalized electricity markets.
